stories.headline: LoC villages await bunkers despite shelling threat
stories.title: LoC villages await bunkers despite shelling threat
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 16: More than a year after Operation Sindoor, residents living along the Line of Control (LoC) in Uri sector of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district say they continue to live under the threat of cross-border shelling, with no new community bunkers visible on the ground. Residents said that despite repeated demands for safe shelters, the construction of new bunkers has not progressed in several border villages. They also claimed that many of the existing bunkers have either deteriorated or are no longer fit to provide adequate protection during shelling. Lal Hussain Kohli, a resident of Charunda village along the LoC, told Rising Kashmir that no new bunker has been constructed in the area since Operation Sindoor. “Not a single new bunker has been built by the government in the last one year. Whatever bunkers we have were constructed nearly five years ago,” he said. Kohli said the village remains vulnerable to cross-border firing and requires functional shelters for the protection of civilians. “There are around eight community bunkers here, but all of them are in a dilapidated condition and cannot be used safely,” he said. Similar concerns were raised by residents of other border villages, including Garkote, Mothal and Silikote. Bashir Ahmad Bhat of Garkote said villagers had received no government support for bunker construction after Operation Sindoor. “If cross-border shelling happens again, where are we supposed to go?” he asked, adding that some families had been forced to construct makeshift shelters using their own limited resources. “We are poor people, but we have no choice. We have to protect our families,” Bhat said. Nadeem Abbasi, an ex-sarpanch of Gawalta village along LoC said that no new bunker had been constructed in the village and residents continued to face serious risks during any escalation along the LoC. “No new bunker has come up here. Our lives continue to remain at risk,” Abbasi said, adding that several older bunkers had also deteriorated and could no longer safely accommodate residents during shelling. The issue of civilian shelters in Uri has remained a concern for years. In 2020, the government had proposed the construction of several community bunkers in the border area. While some were completed, residents said many remained unfinished or inadequate. In May last year, the then Deputy Commissioner, Baramulla, approved the construction of 202 overhead protection trenches in the Uri sector. However, some residents questioned their effectiveness and termed them a waste of public money. “They dug shallow trenches and covered them with wooden planks and mud. Such structures are unsafe during heavy shelling. We need proper concrete bunkers,” said Tariq Hashim, a resident of Kamalkote sector. The issue gained further attention in January this year when then Deputy Commissioner Baramulla Minga Sherpa said that the Home Department had sanctioned more than 500 bunkers to be constructed along the LoC in Uri. However, residents said there was little visible progress on the ground and urged the administration to expedite the construction of durable and fully equipped shelters before any fresh escalation along the LoC. When contacted, Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) Uri Prince Kumar said the matter had already been taken up with the higher authorities. “A proposal in this regard has already been sent to the government,” he told Rising Kashmir.

stories.headline: Only those who support Maoists, separatists are 'dimagi Naxals': Rijiju after Opposition's criticism
stories.title: Only those who support Maoists, separatists are 'dimagi Naxals': Rijiju after Opposition's criticism
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 16: As Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 'dimagi Naxal' remark in his Independence Day speech sparked a war of words between the Opposition and the BJP, Union Minister Kiren Rijiju on Sunday said the PM was not referring to opposition leaders but only to those who support Maoists and separatists and reject the Indian Constitution. Addressing the nation on the 80th Independence Day, Prime Minister Modi on Saturday warned the country about 'dimagi Naxals' who have allegedly entrenched themselves in the system and continue to pose a threat to society by manipulating policies. He cautioned that "armed Naxals may have gone, but dimagi (intellectual) Naxals are lurking around" and called for "identifying and isolating" them. The remark riled the opposition leaders who decried it as an attempt to stigmatise dissent and target those who question the government. In a post on X, Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Rijiju said, "PM Narendra Modi ji didn't say opposition leaders as Dimagi Naxals." "Only following are Dimagi Naxals: 1. Who support Maoists and reject the Indian Constitution. 2. Who stand with separatists & support Article 370. "4. Who want to cut chicken neck to separate North-East from India (sic)," he said in veiled reference to student activist Sarjeel Imam, who is in judicial custody in connection with a case under the anti-terror UAPA law. Imam was arrested on August 25, 2020, and booked under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) for being one of the "masterminds" of the February 2020 riots in northeast Delhi that left 53 people dead and over 700 injured. Congress Rajya Sabha MP Pawan Khera took a jibe at Rijiju with a post on X: "Brother Kiren Rijiju, get your counting right first, then we'll answer. After 1 and 2 comes 3, not 4." "Entire Political Science's kamaal (The marvel of entire political science)," Congress' Jairam Ramesh said, responding to Khera's comment. Earlier, senior Congress leader and former Home Minister P Chidambaram posted on X, "I am proud to be a dimagi Naxal". BJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad condemned Chidambaram's remark, terming it "utterly irresponsible". Addressing a press conference in Patna, Prasad said Prime Minister Modi's reference to "dimagi Naxal" meant those people who sit in air-conditioned rooms in Delhi, Mumbai, Patna and Kolkata and nurture the ideology of Maoism. "They leverage their networks to secure funds and logistical support for the (Naxal) movement. Whenever they find themselves in a tight spot, they appear on television to justify the group's heinous crimes. "And when the public seethes with anger over Maoist atrocities, these individuals pen scathing articles in prominent English newspapers in their defence," Prasad said. Such people are called "dimagi Naxals", the former Union minister added. BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra hit out at Chidambaram, saying although it's late, it is good that the Congress leader has accepted the title of "dimagi Naxal". "Now we know why Naxalism prospered during your tenure as Home Minister and under the UPA government. Now we know why around 2000 policemen and CRPF jawans were killed fighting Naxalism during 2004-14," the BJP MP said in a post on X. "Now, we know why more than 5000 Indians lost their lives to Naxal attacks under your government. Now, we know why as HM, you allowed 92 per cent of Naxal weapons to be looted from police armouries. Now, we know 183 districts remained hostage to Naxal violence in 2013," he added. BJP MP Nishikant Dubey posted an old video of Chidambaram where he can be purportedly heard pitching against "acquiring" nuclear weapons and inducting them into Indian armed forces until there is a "full and proper debate" in the country and in Parliament about its need. "Looking at the state of the world today, tell me if this statement by Chidambaram, a leader of Sonia Gandhi-led Congress, is the statement of a 'dimagi naxal' or not?" Dubey said on X. In a post on X, BJP national general secretary (organisation) B L Santhosh also slammed Chidambaram, saying, "No surprise. He was the PMC (Project Management Consultant ) of Saffron Terrorism - Bhagwa Atankwad project of UPA." BJP's IT department head Amit Malviya said: "'Dimaagi Naxals' has hit them right where it hurts. It is such a delight to see them writhing like snakes in a sandpit".
